title: Pedialyte Popsicles for a Hangover: Do Freezer Pops Help?
excerpt: Do Pedialyte popsicles help a hangover? What's in Pedialyte Freezer Pops, how many to have, how they compare with liquid Pedialyte, a DIY recipe, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Do Pedialyte popsicles help a hangover? What's in the freezer pops, how many to have, a DIY version, and when a rough morning needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Pedialyte popsicles (sold as Pedialyte Freezer Pops) can help with a hangover in one specific way. They get a little fluid, sodium, potassium, and sugar into you when your stomach won't tolerate much else. That makes them most useful on the queasy morning when a full glass of anything comes right back up. What they won't do is fix the headache, the fatigue, or the foggy, poisoned feeling, because those come mostly from how your body processes alcohol, not just from losing fluid. Each pop is small, so treat them as a gentle way to get started on rehydration, not as the whole plan. This guide explains what's actually in them, how many to have, how they compare with drinking Pedialyte or making your own, and when a hangover is really something that needs a doctor.

**The quick rules:** If you're nauseated, let one pop melt slowly in your mouth, wait 10 to 15 minutes, and have another if it stays down. Once your stomach settles, switch to sipping liquid Pedialyte, an electrolyte drink, or water, because you'll need far more fluid than a few pops provide. Add bland food as soon as you can. If you can't keep anything down for most of a day, or you notice signs of serious dehydration or alcohol poisoning, stop self-treating and get medical care.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and product information in plain language. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor or get urgent care if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than about 12 to 24 hours, you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you feel faint or dizzy when you stand, you're confused, your urine is very dark or you've barely urinated all day, or you have severe belly pain. If someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has bluish or pale clammy skin, **call 911**. That can be alcohol poisoning, and no electrolyte product treats it. And if you drink heavily every day and get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or start seeing or hearing things when you stop, that's alcohol withdrawal, not a hangover. It can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than riding it out.

## What Are Pedialyte Popsicles?

Pedialyte is an oral rehydration solution, a carefully balanced mix of water, sugar, and salts. It was originally made for children who were losing fluid to vomiting or diarrhea, and it has since become a popular hangover purchase for adults. Pedialyte Freezer Pops are the same idea in a different shape: individually sealed plastic tubes of electrolyte solution that you freeze and eat like an ice pop.

A few practical things to know:

- **They're small.** Each pop is about 2 fluid ounces (around 60 mL), which is roughly a quarter of a standard cup. Boxes usually hold 16 pops.
- **They come unfrozen.** You buy them at room temperature and put them in the freezer yourself. That means you can keep a box in the cupboard and freeze a few when you need them, but you have to plan an hour or two ahead.
- **They're low in sugar compared with regular ice pops.** The formula follows rehydration principles rather than candy principles, so they taste mildly sweet and a little salty.
- **The flavors are kid-friendly.** Grape, cherry, blue raspberry, and similar. Adults sometimes find them a bit medicinal, though most people describe them as perfectly drinkable (or lickable) when frozen.

People search for "Pedialyte popsicles for adults" because the packaging is clearly aimed at parents. There's nothing child-specific about the solution itself. The same oral rehydration approach is used for adults, and the product label gives directions for both kids and adults. Adults simply need more of it.

## Do Pedialyte Popsicles Help a Hangover?

They help with one part of it. To see why, it helps to know what a hangover actually is.

### What alcohol does to your fluid balance

Alcohol lowers the release of a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone). Vasopressin's job is to tell your kidneys to hold on to water. When it drops, your kidneys let more water go, so you urinate more than you drank. That's the main reason you wake up thirsty with a dry mouth after a night out. If you also sweated on a dance floor, vomited, or had diarrhea, you lost more fluid and salts on top of that.

Rehydrating with something that contains sodium and a little sugar replaces those losses faster than plain water alone, especially if you lost fluid through vomiting or diarrhea. That's the whole reason oral rehydration solutions exist, and it's what a Pedialyte pop offers.

### What dehydration doesn't explain

Here's the part most product marketing glosses over: researchers who study hangovers generally agree that dehydration is only one contributor, and probably not the main one. Studies that measured blood markers of hydration and electrolytes in hungover people have not found that they track closely with how bad the hangover feels. The current scientific view is that hangovers come from several things at once, including:

- **Acetaldehyde**, a toxic by-product your liver makes while breaking down alcohol
- **Inflammation**, as the immune system responds to alcohol and its by-products
- **Poor sleep**, because alcohol fragments the second half of the night
- **Low blood sugar** in some people, especially if they didn't eat
- **Stomach irritation**, since alcohol increases acid and inflames the stomach lining
- **Congeners**, extra compounds in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine

A freezer pop does nothing for acetaldehyde, inflammation, or lost sleep. It does a modest amount for fluid loss and a small amount for blood sugar. So if your main complaint is thirst, a dry mouth, and a dull headache, you may feel noticeably better after rehydrating. If your main complaint is nausea, fatigue, and brain fog, expect a smaller improvement. For a fuller rundown of how long the different symptoms tend to last, see our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last).

### Where the popsicle format genuinely earns its place

The frozen format has a real advantage when you're nauseated. Gulping a big glass of liquid on an upset stomach often triggers more vomiting. Medical advice for rehydrating after vomiting, especially for children, is to take small amounts often rather than a lot at once, and an ice pop enforces that automatically. You can't drink a freezer pop fast. It melts slowly, it's cold (which many people find soothing when they feel sick), and it delivers fluid a little at a time.

That's the honest pitch: Pedialyte popsicles are a good tool for the first hour or two of a queasy hangover, when keeping anything down is the problem. After that, other options do the job more efficiently. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers more ways to settle your stomach.

## What's in a Pedialyte Freezer Pop?

Pedialyte's classic formula is built around the same balance used in medical oral rehydration solutions: enough sodium to help your gut absorb water, some potassium, chloride, and a modest amount of sugar (dextrose). The sugar isn't just for taste. Your small intestine absorbs sodium and glucose together through a shared transporter, and water follows them. That's why a drink with the right ratio of salt and sugar rehydrates you faster than water alone when you've lost a lot of fluid, and why a very sugary drink can actually work less well.

Because each pop is only about 2 ounces, the amounts per pop are small. Roughly speaking, one freezer pop delivers a small fraction of what a full 12-ounce serving of liquid Pedialyte does, something like a sixth. Calories and sugar are low, typically a single-digit number of calories and a gram or two of sugar per pop. Exact values vary slightly by product version and flavor, so check the nutrition panel on your box.

Here's a rough comparison to put the size in perspective:

| | One Pedialyte Freezer Pop | 12 oz liquid Pedialyte | 12 oz glass of water |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fluid | ~2 oz | 12 oz | 12 oz |
| Sodium | Small (about a sixth of a 12 oz serving) | Moderate | Essentially none |
| Sugar | ~1–2 g | Several grams | None |
| Best for | Sipping-style rehydration when nauseated | Steady rehydration once you can keep liquids down | Basic hydration when you aren't badly depleted |
| Speed you can take it | Slow by design | As fast as your stomach allows | As fast as your stomach allows |

The takeaway: the pops use a well-designed formula, but they come in tiny portions. One or two pops isn't meaningful rehydration on its own. They're the on-ramp.

## How Many Pedialyte Popsicles Should You Have for a Hangover?

There's no hangover-specific dose, because Pedialyte isn't a hangover treatment. It's a rehydration product, and the right amount depends on how much fluid you've lost. The box gives general directions for adults and children, and those are a sensible starting point. Follow the label, and keep these practical points in mind:

1. **Start with one, slowly.** Let it melt in your mouth over 10 to 15 minutes rather than biting it.
2. **Wait and see.** If it stays down for 15 minutes or so, have another.
3. **Move to liquids when you can.** Most adults rehydrating after a rough night will need several cups of fluid over the morning. Getting that from 2-ounce pops alone would take a lot of pops. Once your stomach has calmed down, switch to sipping liquid Pedialyte, an electrolyte drink, or water with food.
4. **Don't overthink the upper limit for a single morning.** For a healthy adult, a handful of pops over a few hours isn't a concern. The label directions matter more if you're using Pedialyte for days at a time, or if you have a condition that affects your salt and fluid balance.

**Who should check with a doctor first:** people with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure who have been told to limit sodium, and anyone on a fluid restriction. The sodium in a few pops is modest, but if you've been given specific limits, follow them. People with diabetes should count the sugar, though the amount per pop is small.

## Pedialyte Pops vs Liquid Pedialyte vs Other Options

The freezer pops are one of several ways to get the same basic thing. Here's how they stack up for a hangover.

### Pedialyte Freezer Pops

**Pros:**
- Easiest format to keep down when you're nauseated
- Built-in slow pacing, which reduces the chance of vomiting it back up
- Cold and soothing on a dry, sore throat
- Shelf-stable until you freeze them, so you can keep a box on hand
- Low sugar compared with regular ice pops

**Cons:**
- Small volume per pop, so they can't do the full rehydration job on their own
- Need to be frozen ahead of time (an hour or two at least)
- More expensive per ounce of fluid than liquid Pedialyte or powder packs
- Lots of individual plastic packaging
- Flavors and texture are aimed at kids

### Liquid Pedialyte

Liquid Pedialyte delivers much more fluid per serving and costs less per ounce. It's the better choice once you can keep liquids down. Chilling it helps the taste, and sipping it slowly gets you most of the benefit of the pop without the volume limit. For a deeper look at how it compares with sports drinks, see our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).

### Powder packs

Pedialyte and other brands sell single-serving powders you mix into water. They're cheaper and easier to travel with than bottles. If you plan ahead for a night out, a couple of packets in a drawer cover you without taking up fridge or freezer space. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing.

### Regular ice pops

A standard fruit ice pop gives you cold fluid and sugar, but little or no sodium. If that's all you have, it's still better than nothing for a nauseated stomach. Just know it isn't doing the same job, and follow it with something salty once you can eat.

### Water and a salty snack

For a mild hangover where you mainly feel thirsty, plain water plus a salty food (crackers, toast with a bit of salt, broth) covers much of the same ground as an electrolyte product, for almost nothing. Electrolyte drinks matter most when you've lost a lot of fluid quickly, especially through vomiting or diarrhea. Our roundup of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares more options.

## How to Make Your Own Pedialyte Popsicles

If you don't want to buy freezer pops, you have two easy routes.

### Option 1: Freeze liquid Pedialyte

Pour liquid Pedialyte (any flavor you like) into ice pop molds or an ice cube tray, and freeze for several hours. You get the same formula in a format you control, often for less money. Ice cubes made this way are handy too: you can suck on one at a time if you're very nauseated, or drop them into water.

One note: don't dilute Pedialyte with juice or add sugar to make it taste better. Oral rehydration solutions work because of their specific salt-to-sugar balance. Adding a lot of sugar can make them less effective and may worsen an upset stomach or diarrhea.

### Option 2: A simple homemade rehydration mix

The World Health Organization has long published a basic home recipe for oral rehydration for use when commercial solutions aren't available: about 1 liter of clean water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar, and half a level teaspoon of salt, stirred until dissolved. Measure carefully. Too much salt is the main thing to avoid, and a homemade version is less precise than a commercial product.

You can freeze this in molds the same way. It won't taste like much, so some people add a squeeze of lemon or lime. For a healthy adult with an ordinary hangover, this is a reasonable budget option. For a child, someone who is significantly dehydrated, or anyone with a medical condition, use a commercial product and follow medical advice.

## When to Use Pedialyte Popsicles (and When Not To)

**Good times to reach for one:**
- You woke up nauseated and even water feels like it will come back up
- You've vomited and want to restart fluids gently
- Your mouth and throat are dry and sore, and something cold sounds bearable
- You're in bed and want something easy to keep nearby (freeze a few before you go out)

**Times they aren't the right tool:**
- You feel fine except for a headache and fatigue. Fluid helps a bit, but rest, food, and time do more.
- You can already drink normally. Liquid Pedialyte, an electrolyte drink, or water with food is faster and cheaper.
- You're using them as a reason to keep drinking. Electrolytes don't make extra drinks safer for your liver, your judgment, or your sleep.
- Someone is very drowsy, confused, or hard to wake after drinking. That person needs medical help, not a popsicle, and shouldn't be given anything by mouth if they might choke.

## A Simple Hangover Morning Plan Using Pedialyte Pops

If you've woken up feeling rough and you have a box of freezer pops ready, here's a sensible sequence:

1. **First 30 minutes:** One pop, slowly. Sit upright. Open a window or get some fresh air if you feel queasy.
2. **Next 30 to 60 minutes:** A second pop if the first stayed down. When the nausea eases, start small sips of liquid Pedialyte, an electrolyte drink, or water.
3. **As soon as you can eat:** Something bland with a bit of salt and carbohydrate, like toast, crackers, a banana, rice, or broth. Food helps steady your blood sugar and settles the stomach. Eggs are a good choice if you can face them; see our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).
4. **Through the rest of the morning:** Keep drinking fluids steadily. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you've caught up.
5. **For pain:** If you need a pain reliever, read the label and the alcohol warning first, take it with food, and stick to the standard dose. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen each have their own cautions after drinking, which our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains.
6. **Rest:** Sleep, if you can. Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and a lot of the hangover fog is simply sleep debt.

## What Pedialyte Can't Do

It's worth being clear about the limits, because "Pedialyte for hangovers" gets oversold online.

- **It doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol.** Your liver processes alcohol at its own pace. Fluids, electrolytes, coffee, and cold showers don't change that.
- **It doesn't treat acetaldehyde or inflammation.** These are major drivers of how bad a hangover feels, and rehydration doesn't touch them.
- **It won't sober you up.** If you're still feeling the alcohol, you're still impaired. Don't drive.
- **It doesn't make heavy drinking safer.** Being well hydrated doesn't protect your liver, your heart, or your judgment.

If you find yourself stocking freezer pops because rough mornings are a regular event, the most effective change is upstream: drinking less, pacing with water between drinks, and eating before and during. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence behind them.

## Where DHM Fits In

Electrolytes address fluid loss. They don't address how your body handles alcohol itself, which is where some people look at supplements.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's best described as promising rather than established. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers outright, and it doesn't replace rehydration, food, sleep, or drinking less. Some people take it alongside water and electrolytes as part of a night-out routine.

If you want to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly single-ingredient tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients including electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Pedialyte popsicles are a smart thing to have in the freezer for a nauseated hangover morning. Their small size and slow melt make them one of the easiest ways to restart fluids when your stomach is rebelling, and the formula is properly designed for rehydration. But each pop is only about 2 ounces, so they're a starting point, not the whole fix. Move on to liquid fluids and food as soon as you can, expect them to help with thirst and dry mouth more than with fatigue or brain fog, and know the warning signs that mean it's time to stop self-treating and get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do Pedialyte popsicles help with a hangover?**

They help with the dehydration part of a hangover, and they're especially useful when you're nauseated, because the slow-melting format makes it easier to keep fluids down. They don't treat the other causes of a hangover, such as acetaldehyde, inflammation, and poor sleep, so they won't fix fatigue or brain fog on their own.

**Can adults eat Pedialyte freezer pops?**

Yes. The packaging is aimed at parents, but the rehydration solution isn't child-specific, and the label includes directions for adults. Adults simply need more fluid overall, so treat the pops as a gentle start and follow them with liquid fluids once your stomach allows.

**How many Pedialyte popsicles should I eat for a hangover?**

Follow the directions on the box. A practical approach is to start with one, let it melt slowly, wait about 15 minutes, and have another if it stays down. Because each pop is only about 2 ounces, switch to sipping liquid Pedialyte, an electrolyte drink, or water once you can, rather than trying to rehydrate entirely with pops. If you have kidney or heart problems or are on a sodium or fluid restriction, ask your doctor first.

**Are Pedialyte pops better than drinking Pedialyte?**

Not better, just easier when you're nauseated. Liquid Pedialyte delivers far more fluid per serving and costs less per ounce. The pops are the better choice for the first hour or so when small, slow amounts are all your stomach will accept.

**Can I make my own Pedialyte popsicles?**

Yes. The easiest way is to pour liquid Pedialyte into ice pop molds or an ice cube tray and freeze it. You can also use the World Health Organization's basic home recipe (about 1 liter of clean water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar, and half a level teaspoon of salt) and freeze that. Measure carefully, and don't add extra sugar or juice, because that upsets the balance that makes rehydration solutions work.

**Is Pedialyte or Gatorade better for a hangover?**

Pedialyte has more sodium and potassium and less sugar than standard Gatorade, so it's better designed for rehydration, especially after vomiting or diarrhea. For a mild hangover, though, water plus a salty snack does much of the same job. Our Pedialyte vs Gatorade guide has the side-by-side numbers.

**Do Pedialyte popsicles stop hangover nausea?**

They don't stop nausea directly, but they're one of the easiest ways to rehydrate while you're nauseated, and many people find something cold soothing. If you can't keep anything down, including small amounts of fluid, for more than about 12 to 24 hours, or you're vomiting blood, see a doctor.

**When should I see a doctor instead of treating a hangover at home?**

Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, feel faint when standing, are confused, have very dark urine or have barely urinated, have severe belly pain, or are vomiting blood. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly, has a seizure, or has bluish skin. And if you drink heavily every day and get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that may be alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor's input.
